cases.title: Compare the three dataflow modes.

inputs.question: Compare the three dataflow modes.

expected.user: Compare the three dataflow modes.
expected.expected_standalone_query: Compare data passing through databases, services, and real-time transports in Chapter 3.
expected.reference_answer: Database-mediated flow is simple: one process writes and another reads, but both need database access and database I/O can be too slow for strict latency requirements [N48:P92]. Service-mediated flow is request-driven: a remote service receives a REST/RPC-style request and returns data, supporting independently developed microservices but creating synchronous dependencies [N49:P93] [N50:P94]. A real-time transport introduces a broker or event bus so producers broadcast events and consumers subscribe without direct pairwise requests; this reduces service coupling and better suits data-heavy systems [N50:P95] [N50:P96].

cases.title: How does reservoir sampling work?

inputs.question: How does reservoir sampling work?

expected.user: How does reservoir sampling work?
expected.expected_standalone_query: How does reservoir sampling work?
expected.reference_answer: Keep the first k stream items in a reservoir. For the nth incoming item, draw i uniformly from 1 through n; if i is at most k, replace reservoir item i, otherwise discard the new item [N59:P106]. This gives each observed item probability k/n of being in the reservoir, so the process can stop at any time with a uniform sample [N60:P107].

cases.title: What is data leakage?

inputs.question: What is data leakage?

expected.user: What is data leakage?
expected.expected_standalone_query: What is data leakage in machine learning?
expected.reference_answer: Data leakage occurs when information related to the label enters the prediction features even though the same information will not be available at inference time [N82:P156]. It can produce excellent evaluation results while failing after deployment because the model learned an unavailable shortcut rather than the intended signal [N82:P155].
coverage_points: Data leakage occurs when information related to the label enters the prediction features even though the same information will not be available at inference time .
It can produce excellent evaluation results while failing after deployment because the model learned an unavailable shortcut rather than the intended signal .

cases.title: How do I prevent the common kinds?

inputs.question: How do I prevent the common kinds?

expected.user: How do I prevent the common kinds?
expected.expected_standalone_query: How can common forms of data leakage be prevented?
expected.reference_answer: For time-correlated data, split by time so future conditions do not enter training [N83:P157]. Split before scaling or imputing, then compute statistics only from the training split and apply them to validation and test data [N83:P158]. Detect duplicates before and after splitting, oversample only after the split, and keep strongly correlated groups such as scans from one patient in the same split [N83:P159].

Split before scaling or imputing, then compute statistics only from the training split and apply them to validation and test data .

inputs.question: Now explain quantization.

expected.user: Now explain quantization.
expected.expected_standalone_query: Explain model quantization.
expected.reference_answer: Quantization compresses a model by representing parameters with fewer bits. Moving from 32-bit floats to 16-bit values halves parameter memory, while integer representations can reduce it further [N113:P229]. cases.title: Summarize Batch Prediction Versus Online Prediction in Chapter 7.

inputs.question: Summarize Batch Prediction Versus Online Prediction in Chapter 7.

expected.user: Summarize Batch Prediction Versus Online Prediction in Chapter 7.
expected.expected_standalone_query: Summarize the Batch Prediction Versus Online Prediction section in Chapter 7.
expected.reference_answer: Online prediction generates a response when a request arrives and is optimized for low latency; batch prediction generates predictions periodically, stores them, and is optimized for throughput [N106:P217] [N106:P220]. Online prediction can use only batch features or combine batch and streaming features, so online and streaming are not synonyms [N106:P219]. Batch remains useful when results are not immediately needed or when precomputation avoids slow inference, but it is less responsive and requires anticipated requests [N107:P221] [N107:P222]. Separate batch and streaming feature pipelines can diverge [N108:P224], motivating unified processing or feature-store infrastructure [N108:P225].

cases.title: Why is representing every token as a one-hot vector a poor choice?

inputs.question: Why is representing every token as a one-hot vector a poor choice?

expected.user: Why is representing every token as a one-hot vector a poor choice?
expected.expected_standalone_query: Why is representing every token as a one-hot vector a poor choice?

expected_evidence.why: Cosine similarity compares the angle between vectors, and one-hot vectors are all orthogonal to one another, so no two tokens can be similar. The Token representations slide naming naive one-hot encoding is on screen.

expected.reference_answer: Similarity between tokens is usually measured with cosine similarity, which looks at the angle between the vectors. One-hot vectors are all orthogonal to each other, so every pair of tokens looks equally unrelated and the representation carries no meaning.

cases.title: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?

inputs.question: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?

expected.user: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?
expected.expected_standalone_query: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?

expected_evidence.why: Direct links between tokens destroy the sense of order an RNN got from processing one at a time, so position encodings are added to carry the position of a word in the sequence.

expected.reference_answer: Because attention gives every token a direct link to every other one, which throws away the ordering an RNN got for free by processing the sequence one step at a time. Position encodings are added to carry where each word sits in the sequence.

cases.title: Candidate assessment — proximity-weak
Candidate assessment — proximity-mixed

expected.answer: First I'd clarify the maximum search radius and whether users can change it. I'd also ask about expected traffic and how fresh business updates must be. I'll assume location searches are latency-sensitive and business changes can be asynchronous.

cases.title: Candidate assessment — proximity-strong

expected.answer: I'd clarify the search contract: input location, allowed radius, pagination, business details, and whether results update as a user moves. Then scale and SLOs—traffic, peak geographic skew, latency, and availability. For writes, I'd ask whether owner edits must be real time; if next-day visibility is acceptable, I can separate write ingestion from a read-optimized geo index. I'd also establish privacy and retention expectations for precise location.

cases.title: Candidate assessment — rag-weak

expected.answer: I would use a vector database.

cases.title: Candidate assessment — rag-mixed

expected.answer: I'd clarify the document types, corpus size, and how often content changes. I'd ask what kinds of questions users submit, how fresh answers need to be, and the latency target. I would also confirm how much retrieved context can fit in the model prompt.

cases.title: Candidate assessment — rag-strong

expected.answer: I'd clarify the corpus, formats, scale, and update cadence; the query types; and what counts as relevant retrieval. Then I'd establish freshness and latency targets, the context and cost budget, and how the assistant should respond when retrieval is empty or contradictory. I would ask for offline retrieval and grounded-answer success criteria before choosing chunking, embeddings, or a vector store.
